The M stands for Michael, Mike to his friends. And last night he became the oldest author to win the Booker prize for fiction, for his 13th novel, The End of Everything. Our interview is delayed because of wifi issues, which is fitting given that the novel is about – among many things – what happens when non-human intelligence takes over.

The End of Everything is the first sci-fi novel to have won the prize in its 58-year history, which is almost as long as Harrison has been writing. “It’s interesting,” he replies, when asked if he feels vindicated, “that something that has an SF-adjacent feel can be regarded as a serious book and given the Booker prize. My problem has always been that I don’t believe in genre. I don’t believe in it in any way.” He gently wags his finger at me. pg:https://www.theguardian.com/books/202.desc: After years on the margins, Harrison’s win for this resonantly disturbing dystopia brings the visionary writer the recognition he deserves
paras: Some have balked at a novel where none of the characters knows what’s going on, and the prose scrupulously refuses to make things any clearer for the reader. “None of this made any sense to Marnie. In that, she shared the situation of around 8 billion other human beings on the planet.” Harrison has always traded in unknowing: in Climbers, his brilliant 1989 novel about his passion for rock climbing, by the end all the main character has learned is that “I didn’t know anything about anything”.

But Harrison’s own description of The End of Everything – “What happens when all of our expectations and explanations of the world become an ongoing disaster, but we still have to make a life?” – is a strikingly topical question for 2026. It’s precisely the uncertainty, the sudden violence, the sense that something incomprehensible is happening out of the corner of one’s eye, that makes it resonate so deeply. In the postwar period, writers such as JG Ballard and Nevil Shute channelled fears of ecological breakdown and nuclear armageddon. Now, it’s Everything.

Harrison started out in science fiction – a genre famously overlooked by the Booker – publishing his first short story in Science Fantasy magazine in 1966, and becoming part of the 70s SF New Wave with Ballard and Michael Moorcock. You can find the operatic wonder and alienation of space opera in The End of Everything, though here trained on Earth: in the wake of the iGhetti, “the night was crawling with new constellations”. (A sentence that made me think of Elon Musk’s thousands of satellites.) Phillip the beachcomber – the broken man looking for revelation and a change of fortune in his shoreline discoveries – is reminiscent of the noirish space wanderers in Harrison’s back catalogue.

Whether the actions of Mr. Hegseth, the first target of the surging Democrats whose victories last week will thrust them into majority power in the House in January, meet the Article II, Section 4, Constitutional impeachment requirements will be at the centre of the searing debate that is beginning to unfold. But this “moment in history,” as Mr. Ford would put it, will examine the frontiers of the definition of “treason, bribery or other high crimes and misdemeanors” that the country’s 18th-century founders set forth.

paras: If Michael Carrick’s departure as head coach of Manchester United is confirmed, Mauricio Pochettino is reportedly the man tasked with turning the fortunes of the Old Trafford club around.

pg:https://www.cbc.ca/news/entertainment.desc: Stacy Keach, one of America's finest stage actors who became best known for playing scruffy private eye Mike Hammer on TV and whose career was nearly derailed after he was imprisoned in 1984 for trying to smuggle cocaine into Britain, died Tuesday. paras: Keach died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, "after a long and difficult battle with a serious heart condition and heart failure," his wife, Malgosia Tomassi Keach, said in a statement. Keach had previously suffered a heart attack onstage in Chicago in June 2017.

Unwilling to do the same thing over and over, Keach left behind a crazy quilt of roles, playing a stoner cop on film, King Lear onstage and also narrating World's Most Amazing Videos on TV. He played a deranged colonel in The Ninth Configuration (also known as Twinkle, Twinkle Killer Kane), led the TV show Titus, had a role in Alexander Payne's Oscar-nominated drama Nebraska and played a New York archbishop in a recurring role on the CBS police drama Blue Bloods. pg:https://www.theguardian.com/books/202.desc: Kazuo Ishiguro, Jeff VanderMeer, Olivia Laing and other writers weigh in on the publishing world’s genre wars
paras: Ella CreamerWed 11 Nov 2026 16.44 GMTLast modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 18.42 GMTShare Prefer the Guardian on Google As M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction, with a decidedly fantastical book.

His fans, many leading authors among them, are thrilled. “For decades it was a standard – and correct – nerd whine to point out that sentence for sentence, book for book, Harrison was one of the greatest writers out there, full stop, but that ‘mainstream’ prizes never reflected that,” says China Miéville, who last week won the Goldsmiths prize with his 1,200-page speculative novel The Rouse. Back in 2002, Miéville wrote that Harrison not having won a Booker by that point proved “the bankruptcy and back-slapping generic snobbery of the literary establishment”. Now, he says: “I am so delighted, for Harrison, and for fiction.”

While some past Booker-winning authors draw heavily on SF – Margaret Atwood, Kazuo Ishiguro, Ian McEwan – Harrison is the first winner from the “bona fide SF” sphere, said Booker prize foundation chief executive Gaby Wood on Monday. The Pulitzer and the Nobel rarely take notice of SF either, though the latter has honoured Ishiguro and Doris Lessing – both of whom are considered literary writers who dabble in SF, rather than purists, and thus perhaps considered more palatable to a wider reading public.
